To the PRINTER.
As every thing that is exhibited to the public is
open equally to censure and applause, there
needs no further preface to any remarks upon this
subject, than just to observe it would be abusing the
patience of your readers to permit them to be re-
criticised by every person that can form no judge-
ment of their own, and yet are dissatisfied with an-
other's. I believe if the observation that are made
by the spectators upon the pictures now exhibiting
were published, they would shew that the people
have at least as good a taste as their artists have skill.
Public exhibitions were well calculated for the im-
provement of both; but if we believe the judge-
ment of the former, the present exhibitions do not
do much honour to the London school of painting.
Of the PICTURES exhibited in SPRING-GARDEN.
No. 4. It's a good landscape; but it is never seen
in a rainbow where one colour ends and another
begins.
No. 20. It is a question whether the painter has
succeeded better in the child or greyhound; he has
succeeded so well in each. It is much in the stile of
Miss Reid; and there is a picture of her's that would
do well for its companion; the boy being turned into
a girl, and the dog into a kitten.
No. 38. The painter seems to have had death so
much in her eye, when she painted the dead Sigis-
munda, that she has left no life in any of the other
figures. That is a bad medium for a painter to see
through, whose art lies (I might say) in giving life
to inanimate substances. The girl, with her hand
to her face, seems as if she was only making belief
to cry; but that perhaps may have been intended,
though such burlesque none but Hogarth would ad-
mit in historical painting.
No. 39. Shews what difference there may be in the
same painter, whose she attempts a piece within her
abilities, that where she would exceed them.
No. 43. The painter that would attemps, must ei-
ther have succeeded greatly, or as greatly failed.
This gentleman has, I suppose, chose to do the lat-
ter, or he would not have put it in so bad a light.
No. 46. Achilles undoubtedly should be the prin-
cipal figure; if he is well represented, the painter
will secure his piece from contempt. The agency of
Achilles' grief is, I believe, well enough conceived
in the posture it has thrown him into: but take the
whole painting together, it is certainly not a capital
performace. The figures are too many for the
piece, and too much crowded. The painter seems
to have entertained the vulgar notion about the look
of an old Grecian in the antiquated portions he has
given us: there is more merit in the women. Pa-
troclus must have been brought all dirty to Achilles,
and he is not likely to have staid to have had him
washed before he lamented over him. The painter
possibly never saw a dead body-he had heard it was
of a pale colour, and therefore he made it so; but a
body killed in action, and that has not been before
made palid by sickness, would not yet be destitute
of the colour of life, though the muscles and veins
would lose their tensions. The blood does not turn
white, because its circulation is stopped, nor the
tures might possibly have as much success as some of
Mr. Hogarth's; and Mr. Golder may very likely do
for the purpose.
No. 145, 146. The Pingo's are known to be excel-
lent artists.
No. 152, 153. Miss Reid succeeds as usual, and
draws with a delicacy that shews how well her sex is
calculated to excel in this amiable act. Of the two

Quere, how far is it allowable for a painter, when he
vies in the scene he undertakes with a poet, to de-
part from the description of the latter?
No. 239. Would a person pay a compliment to
Mr. Strange, or not, was he to say that his genius
could not receive improvement in Italy. Quere,
How comes the ostrich to be an emblem of justice?
I ask for Information.
No. 250. There may be less genius in this kind of
representation, than in a piece of painting; as there
is less merit in making a wax doll, than in painting
a little Jesus; but however, this basket fruit is
enough to make one's teeth water when one sees it;
possibly the lady might do so too.
Of rhe EXHIBITION in MAIDEN-LANE.
No. 6 . Is good.
No. 35 to 47. All excellent; There is said to be
a sameness in the Chevalier's paintings; so much
the better, if the sameness is to excel alike in all.
No. 58, &c. Mr. Collet seems to have a great
deal of comic humour; engraving from these pic-
little boys the eldest seems to take after the father,
and look almost as heavy as himself; and the young-
est after the mother.
No. 158. If likeness is a merit in a portrait, Mr.
Atkinson of Greenwich can shew how well the pain-
ter has succeeded. Aut erasmus aut diabolus, either
Dunce, Scotus, or a school-master.
A fruit piece of two peaches and a nectarine upon
a real pewter plate, is most admirable. There for
no number to it as I could see; but the artist need
not have been ashamed to have published his name
nor the socierty to have numbered it in this cata-
logue.
